interactions.summary: Jiang continues the hardship answer by describing long-lasting trauma from racist high school bullying, years of poverty, disgust at public-relations work, and a hard-won refusal to fear cancellation or hardship because truth matters more than comfort.

Sneako praises Jiang and proposes future collaborations involving Professor Morandi and others, Jiang calls the Iranian interlocutor courageous, and the exchange widens into possible panels with David Icke, whom Jiang says he wants to question and learn from.
Sneako closes this thematic stretch by returning to Jiang's earlier emphasis on unity and calling these panels a real step toward it.

speaker_notes.note: Jiang's line equating public relations with prostitution is deliberately inflammatory. It should be preserved as his moral rejection of institutional messaging work, not softened into a generic career preference.
The transcript gives the collaborator's name as 'Professor Morandi.' Preserve that surface form rather than normalizing it from memory.

claims.claim: Jiang says the trauma of his Canadian high school years lasted decades, producing recurring nightmares up to age forty, but that the adversity also made him resilient and willing to take hard, unconventional risks.
claims.temporal_scope: Biographical reflection stated on 2026-05-18 about adolescence and its later effects.

claims.claim: He says he stayed true to himself through years of poverty and refused to sell out into public-relations work, which he portrays as morally degrading and incompatible with sleep or self-respect.
claims.temporal_scope: Biographical and moral claim stated on 2026-05-18 about earlier career choices.

claims.claim: Jiang says he worked for the United Nations for six months as a public-relations officer, found it among the worst experiences of his life, and quit because he could not sleep at night.
claims.temporal_scope: Biographical employment claim stated on 2026-05-18 about an earlier period.

claims.claim: He says the past year marked a financial turning point because his Substack began making good money, yet he remains unafraid of poverty or cancellation because speaking truth matters more than income.
claims.temporal_scope: Recent financial update and ethical stance stated on 2026-05-18 about the past year.

claims.claim: Jiang says he would welcome a conversation with David Icke because they agree on much, and he thinks Icke knows more than he does about energy harvesting, elite-demon contracts, and the new UFO conversation.

signature_moments.moment: The bullied child who dreamt nightly of humiliation becomes the adult who is no longer afraid of the hard road and now treats that trauma as the forge of wisdom.
signature_moments.source_phrase: this adversity made me who I am today
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It completes the packet's suffering-to-resilience arc in Jiang's own biographical terms.

signature_moments.moment: Public relations is denounced as a kind of prostitution, a profession so spiritually deforming that it cost him sleep and had to be abandoned.
signature_moments.source_phrase: public relations is being a prostitute
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is one of the packet's sharpest Jiang formulations about integrity, institutions, and self-betrayal.

signature_moments.moment: The man who knows poverty stops fearing cancellation because once destitution has already been lived, truth becomes cheaper than compromise.
signature_moments.source_phrase: I'm not afraid of being poor
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It distills Jiang's late-interview ethic of independence from public punishment.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's phrase for staying true to oneself, speaking the truth, and continuing the struggle even under threat of cancellation or renewed poverty.
